newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS-Rate speculation to fuel Germany,Italy.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS-Rate speculation to fuel Germany,Italy.

text.p: Speculation of lower interest rates in Europe has largely been discounted by bond investors but there is still value to be had in the short end of the German and Italian markets, analysts said on Friday.

On Thursday, comments from Bundesbank official Hans-Juergen Krupp that the Bundesbank could not ignore German economic weakness, fuelled speculation that a cut in the German repo rate might be on the way.
In Italy, the market is expecting the Bank of Italy to cut interest rates, possibly in early February, analysts said.
"Germany will lead the way," said Brian Venables, senior bond analyst at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett in Amsterdam.

"It has weaker growth than many of its surrounding countries. So although you can expect other countries to follow any German cut, it is possible their cuts will not be as big and that clearly puts the advantage on German Bobls," he said.
Venables said the Bundesbank was master of the art of keeping interest rate expectations going for longer than anyone would think possible.

"All it would take would be a negligible cut, say 10 or 20 basis points, to actually fuel a much more intensive debate," he said. "And as long as people are always looking for lower rates, the markets can always perform."
The German repo rate has been held at 3.0 percent since it was cut in August.

Ifty Islam, European bond strategist at Merrill Lynch in London, said although Euromark interest rate futures had rallied, they were not really discounting any further cut in the repo rate so still offered some value.
"From a trading perspective, the pressures on the Bundesbank to ease will persist particularly from France," he said.
The French intervention rate at 3.15 percent is currently 15 basis points above the German repo rate.

"If the Bank of France cuts its intervention rate down to three percent the pressure will then mount on the Bundesbank to to oblige the French," said Islam. "That expectation is already pushing Euromarks higher and it will reflect in the weakness of the mark."

But Graham McDevitt, senior analyst at Paribas Capital Markets in London, said rather than anticipating a rate cut the Euromark strip was now becoming more relaxed about the overall course of monetary policy right through 1997.
"That is what has helped the overall short end to fall," he said.
Outside core Europe, analaysts said the Italian and Spainsh short ends both offered value, but on a relative basis Italy was the more attractive of the two being farther behind in the easing cycle.

The Bank of Spain made a surprise 25 basis point cut in its repo rate on Thursday, bringing it down to 6.0 percent. While the Bank of Italy has held its discount rate at 7.5 percent since October, and a further cut is widely anticipated.

"In Italy, the market is expecting big cuts. A 50 to 75 basis point minimum sometime in early February," said McDevitt. "The yield curve has steepened in the last couple of months in anticipation of this."
Islam said he also favoured being long of Italy.

"The major frustration that many traders have felt so far is that the Bank of Italy has been dragging its heals and overnight money rates are so high that to maintain a position at the short end is costing them quite a lot," he said. "We still think it is worth persisting with it."
